problem: The rule as written says that any object whose size is known at compile time can be reserved in the static data region. A student can read this as 'a local int whose size is known goes into static data', which is false: an ordinary local lives in the activation record on the stack. Compile-time-known size is necessary but not sufficient for static storage; the storage class (global, local, dynamic) decides the region.
fix: Rewrite as: 'A global or static object whose size is known at compile time is reserved in the static data region at a fixed address. A local with a fixed size is not put in static data; it is placed at a fixed offset inside its activation record, which sits on the stack.'

problem: Calling the fixed-offset placement of a local 'static allocation in the simple sense' clashes with standard usage, where a local in an activation record is stack allocation and 'static allocation' means a fixed storage location for the whole run (typically globals and statics).
fix: Say instead: 'The offset is fixed before the program starts, but the storage itself is created and destroyed with each call, so this is stack allocation, not static allocation. Chapter 5.3 gives the three allocation strategies.'
